ai.intro: LordOS's selection of AI tools: agents that code with you, editors, and engines that run models and turn speech into text on this computer. Apps whose maker has a signed repository come from it, with the maker's key pinned by LordOS; the others come from LordOS's signed repository, built by LordOS from verified sources or copied after checking the maker's signature.
ai.notListed: {name} is in LordOS's catalog but not in this computer's package lists yet. Fetch the lists again to bring it.
ai.refresh: Some of these aren't in the package lists yet: check for updates in Updates to fetch them.
ai.sourceIntro: {name} comes from {vendor}'s own repository. Installing it adds that repository to this computer, with {vendor}'s signing key that LordOS's catalog pins: from then on its updates come from {vendor}, checked with that key, over HTTPS.
ai.title: Artificial Intelligence
commercial.drivers: Drivers for your graphics card are offered in For this computer when LordOS finds the card.
commercial.intro: Free-of-charge apps whose source code isn't public: browsers, music, games and drivers from their makers. LordOS checks that each one comes from its maker, signed with the key LordOS pins, but can't review or fix what they do; they get the same firewall and permissions as any other Linux app.
off.done: {name} is deactivated: it left the launcher, the Dock and search, and does nothing in the background. Activate it here whenever you want it back.
off.none: No app is deactivated. A LordOS app you don't use can be deactivated here: it leaves the launcher, the Dock and search, and stops working in the background.
off.noticeBody: Activate it to open it. You can deactivate it again in Store → Installed.
off.refused.backup: Backups is restoring or deleting a backup. Wait until it finishes.
off.refused.core: {name} is part of LordOS and can't be deactivated.
off.refused.open: {name} is still open with unsaved changes. Close its window first.
off.refused.vm: A virtual machine is running. Shut it down in Machines first: deactivating never stops a running machine.
remote.intro: Remote access apps from makers outside LordOS, such as a private network that joins your devices wherever they are. They aren't LordOS's Remote Desktop on port 5673. Some install a system service that starts with the computer and isn't held to the firewall's per-app rules. LordOS checks that each one comes from its maker, but can't review or fix what they do.
remove.wouldRemoveLordOS: Removing this package would also remove LordOS itself, so the Store won't do it.
suites.intro: Open source apps and suites from other projects that we think are worth having. Each one comes from its maker: from the maker's signed repository, with the key LordOS pins, or from the maker's own package, which LordOS keeps with a pinned checksum. A suite's launcher may then download its apps from its maker. LordOS doesn't review or fix what they do; they get the same firewall and permissions as any other Linux app.

suggest.nvidiaDriver.detail: Right now it uses nouveau, the free driver included with LordOS. The vendor's driver ({packages}) usually gives better 3D performance and power management.
suggest.nvidiaDriver.note.nouveau: Until you install it, the free nouveau driver stays in use; removing the package goes back to it.
suggest.nvidiaDriver.note.older: Cards older than about 2014 aren't supported by this driver version; keep the free driver on them. The LordOS desktop hasn't been tested with this driver yet.
suggest.nvidiaDriver.note.secureBoot: The driver is built for your kernel on this computer (DKMS) and again after every kernel update. With Secure Boot on, you have to enroll its signing key at the next restart, or the driver won't load.

formats.intro: These formats belong to their makers, but every driver below is free software, at no cost. Nothing is installed until you go on.

formats.optional: Also add APFS. It builds a driver for your kernel and adds about 500 MB of compilers and headers.
multiarch.title: 32-bit system libraries
multiarch.body: {name} needs 32-bit system libraries; LordOS will enable them. The package engine can then install 32-bit (i386) packages from Debian next to the 64-bit ones, signed and checked like any other package. Only what {name} needs is installed.
suggest.studioCamera.title: LordOS Studio Camera
suggest.studioCamera.detail: Gives every app, browsers and video calls included, the “LordOS Studio” camera with your effects: background blur or a picture behind you ({packages}).
suggest.studioCamera.unavailable: {packages} isn't in this computer's package sources.
suggest.studioCamera.note.dkms: On a PC its kernel module is built for your kernel on this computer (DKMS), which brings about 500 MB of compilers and kernel headers, and again after every kernel update. On a Raspberry Pi it comes with the LordOS kernel.
suggest.studioCamera.note.secureBoot: With Secure Boot on, you have to enroll the module’s signing key at the next restart, or the camera won’t appear.
suggest.studioCamera.note.obs: It also adds a second camera device, “OBS Virtual Camera”, so OBS Studio’s own virtual camera works beside LordOS Studio.
suggest.mok.title: One more step at the next restart
suggest.mok.body: Secure Boot is on, so what this item installed loads only after its signing key is enrolled. LordOS prepares the key and gives you a one-time password to type on a blue screen at the next restart.
suggest.mok.pending: The key will be enrolled at the next restart. If you no longer have the password, get a new one.
suggest.mok.passwordHint: Write it down now: it’s shown only once and isn’t saved anywhere.
suggest.mok.steps: Restart, and when the blue screen appears, press a key within 10 seconds. Then choose Enroll MOK → Continue → Yes, type this password and choose Reboot.
